title: Governance, Compliance and Medical Device Security

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare
children.blurb: An AI enablement audit in healthcare examines whether a clinical or operational setting can safely adopt, run, and oversee artificial intelligence systems.

children.name: Local Models for Patient Data
children.blurb: Local models for patient data are machine learning systems that process protected health information on hardware controlled by a healthcare organization, rather than sending it to a third-party cloud.

children.name: Software as a Medical Device
children.blurb: Software as a Medical Device covers software intended for medical purposes without being part of a physical device.

children.name: Bias in Clinical Triage
children.blurb: Bias in clinical triage refers to systematic differences in how an AI system assigns urgency, acuity, or priority to patients based on characteristics such as race, sex, age, language, insurance status, or disability.

children.name: Security of Connected Medical Devices
children.blurb: Security of connected medical devices covers the protection of networked clinical hardware, from infusion pumps and patient monitors to imaging systems and implantable devices, against unauthorized access, data interception, and manipulation.

sections.body: This section covers the practical governance of medical AI, from checking whether a hospital is ready to use a model to keeping patient data and connected devices safe. Artificial intelligence is now being used to read scans, suggest triage priorities, draft clinical notes, and monitor device traffic for anomalies. The work here is not about building new algorithms, it is about auditing existing tools, running models on local hardware, clearing software as a medical device, testing for bias in triage, and securing devices that send data over a network. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models, which gives a sense of how many systems now need this kind of oversight. These pages describe the checks and controls that sit around those models rather than the models themselves.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The field has moved from policy discussion to concrete audits and device submissions, but many problems remain unsolved. Enablement audits can now measure whether a clinic has the data, staff, and logging needed to use a model safely, yet there is no single accepted standard for passing one. Local models for patient data are technically workable on modern hardware, but they still struggle with the cost of running large models and the loss of accuracy compared with cloud systems. Software as a medical device clearance is well defined in some regions, but the rules change as models learn after deployment, and regulators are still catching up. Bias in clinical triage is documented and measurable, but fixing it without breaking performance for other groups is not solved. Connected device security has basic protections like encryption and patching, but many older devices cannot be updated and remain exposed.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader should start with The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare to see how an organization decides whether it is ready to use any of these tools. Local Models for Patient Data then explains one way to reduce privacy risk by keeping records on site, which connects directly to the audit's data controls. Software as a Medical Device covers the formal clearance path for tools that diagnose or treat, and it matters for any model that passes an audit and goes into clinical use. Bias in Clinical Triage looks at a specific high risk use where an unfair model can change who gets care first, so it should be read alongside the clearance page. Security of Connected Medical Devices closes the loop by covering the hardware that feeds data to these models, because a secure model is not enough if the monitor or pump sending data is compromised.
